metadata.title: Linear vs. Logistic Regression, Oversimplified
metadata.note: Fresh free ai-explainer. GATE P intentionally unsigned; no audio generated.

beats.narration_text: Linear regression and logistic regression share a skeleton, then answer different questions. One predicts an amount. The other predicts a probability. This is Liam, in for Bear. The confusing name hides a clean design choice: keep the weighted sum, then change what happens at the output. Let us make that fork visible.

show.event: Claude composer opens; greeting 'Namaste, Liam'
the comparison prompt types in
send arms; running text reads 'choosing the output…'
answered lines land: number / probability / choose by target

props.command: Explain linear and logistic regression with one shared weighted-score pipeline. Show when the output should be a number and when it should be a probability.
output: choose from the target, not the name

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. Both methods combine inputs using learned weights. Linear regression leaves that score as a number, useful for quantities like price or temperature. Logistic regression bends the score through an S-shaped function, turning it into a probability for a class such as yes or no. Same engine room; different dashboard.

show.event: spark line: 'Same score. Different output.'
feature chips flow into one weighted-sum box
the path forks left to a number line and right to a sigmoid
left resolves to '$420k'; right resolves to '0.82 yes'

production_viz.label: shared weighted score
production_viz.mechanic: one score forks into numeric and probabilistic outputs

beats.narration_text: Start with the target, not the algorithm menu. If the answer can naturally keep moving along a number line, you have a regression target: tomorrow's demand, a house price, a temperature. If the answer is membership in a category, you have classification: churn or stay, fraud or legitimate. Logistic regression models the probability of that category, then a separate threshold can turn probability into a decision.

show.event: a target card enters a two-branch decision gate
continuous branch fills with price / demand / temperature
category branch fills with churn / fraud / approve
probability appears before a movable threshold and decision

production_viz.label: target-type framework
production_viz.mechanic: continuous versus categorical target, with probability separated from decision

beats.narration_text: Take house size and price. Plot the sales, fit a line, then use that line to estimate a new home's price. The vertical gaps are residuals, and ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimize the sum of their squares. That is the contract: predict a quantity and pay heavily for large misses. The line can output any real number, including foolish ones outside the data range.

show.event: house-size versus price axes and observed sales draw on
a fitted line sweeps through the cloud
residual segments drop from points to the line
a new home's x-position projects to an illustrative predicted price
the line extrapolates beyond the observed range and gains a warning tag

production_viz.label: ordinary least squares
production_viz.mechanic: fit line, reveal residuals, predict a continuous value
production_viz.note: schematic data and illustrative currency only

beats.narration_text: Now change the target to whether a customer churns. A straight line is awkward: probabilities should not wander below zero or above one. Logistic regression keeps the weighted score, then sends it through the sigmoid. Low scores squeeze toward zero, high scores toward one, and the middle stays sensitive. The result is a probability estimate; a threshold, such as one half, creates the class label.

show.event: binary observations appear at zero and one
a straight line crosses outside the probability band and is rejected
the line transforms into a bounded sigmoid
one customer maps to probability 0.73
a movable 0.5 threshold turns probability into 'churn'

production_viz.label: sigmoid probability
production_viz.mechanic: weighted score is bounded to zero-one, then thresholded

beats.narration_text: The output change also changes the fitting objective. Linear regression usually minimizes squared residuals: distance from each observed number to the predicted number. Logistic regression fits class probabilities by maximizing likelihood, equivalently minimizing log loss. Confidently assigning low probability to what actually happened is punished hard. That is why logistic regression is not merely linear regression with answers clipped between zero and one.

show.event: two aligned fitting panels appear
left residual lengths square into a running loss bowl
right probability chips meet observed zero/one labels
a confident wrong probability triggers a steep terracotta penalty
'different objective' locks across both panels

production_viz.label: least squares versus log loss
production_viz.mechanic: two losses respond differently to errors

beats.narration_text: Now the cleanup. A straight relationship can miss curves, interactions, and changing variance. Logistic probabilities can be badly calibrated, and a one-half threshold may be wrong when false positives and false negatives have different costs. Both models can extrapolate badly, inherit biased data, and mistake association for causation. Their simplicity is a feature only when diagnostics and held-out data say the assumptions are useful.

show.event: four stress-test tiles fill the frame: curve, calibration, threshold, causation
a straight fit visibly misses a curved pattern
predicted 0.8 group resolves to fewer than 80% positives, flagged 'check calibration'
threshold slider moves as error costs change
correlation arrow is stopped before a causal arrow

production_viz.label: assumption stress test
production_viz.note: calibration mismatch is schematic, not measured

beats.narration_text: The verdict. Linear regression predicts a continuous quantity by fitting a weighted sum, commonly with squared error. Logistic regression uses a weighted sum to model class probability through a logistic link, commonly with log loss. Choose by the target and the decision you need. Then test residuals, calibration, thresholds, and performance on data the model never saw.

show.event: Claude artifact page opens with the comparison
linear line highlights: 'quantity'
logistic line highlights: 'class probability'
diagnostic line fills: 'validate the assumptions'

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this in: take one dataset with a continuous target and one with a binary target. Fit linear regression to the first and logistic regression to the second. Visualize predictions, residuals, probabilities, and a movable decision threshold. Then audit four things: target type, loss, extrapolation, and calibration. This prompt turns the names into observable behavior. Look for where each model becomes confidently wrong, not merely where it fits.
